bullets: 1.1 Day, night and the spinning Earth
1.2 The Moon and its phases
1.3 Seasons and Earth's tilt
Goal: explain what you see overhead using only a few simple ideas
slides.notes: This chapter is about what you can see with your own eyes, no equipment needed. We will find that three simple facts explain almost everything: Earth spins, the Moon orbits Earth, and Earth's axis is tilted. Keep those three in mind as we go.
slides.title: Chapter 1 Agenda: Looking Up

bullets: The Sun, Moon and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west
Really, Earth **rotates** (spins) once about every 24 hours
Analogy: on a merry-go-round, the park seems to swirl past you
The spin axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles
slides.notes: Ancient observers reasonably concluded the sky turned around them. The modern explanation is that the ground under us turns. Rotation means spinning around an axis, and Earth's axis runs through the poles.
slides.title: The Sky Seems to Move, but You Are Moving

bullets: The Sun lights half of Earth at any moment
Your location turns into the lit half at sunrise and out of it at sunset
Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun appears to move east to west
Time zones exist because different places face the Sun at different times
slides.notes: Picture a lamp shining on a ball: one half is lit, one half is dark. Spin the ball and each spot on its surface passes from light to dark and back. Earth spins eastward, which is why the Sun appears to climb in the east.
slides.title: Day and Night

bullets: Stars also rise and set because of Earth's spin
Stars are far beyond the Moon and Sun, so their patterns stay fixed relative to each other
Near the North Pole direction, stars appear to circle a point near **Polaris**, the North Star
Different stars are visible in different seasons because Earth orbits the Sun
slides.notes: Stars keep the same patterns, called constellations, night after night. Polaris sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole, so it barely moves while other stars circle it. Over a year, Earth's position on its orbit changes which stars are in the night sky.
slides.title: Stars and the Night Sky

bullets: An **orbit** is the curved path one object takes around another
The Moon circles Earth about once every 27 days
The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight
Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun
slides.notes: The Moon is a rocky ball that shines only by reflected sunlight, like a ball under a lamp. Always half of it faces the Sun and is lit. What changes over the month is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth.
slides.title: The Moon Orbits Earth

bullets: A **phase** is the portion of the Moon's lit half that we see
New Moon: the Moon is between Earth and Sun, so its lit side faces away from us
Full Moon: Earth is roughly between Moon and Sun, so we see the whole lit face
The cycle from new Moon to new Moon takes about 29.5 days
slides.notes: Phases are not caused by Earth's shadow. They come from our changing viewing angle on the lit half. The cycle takes about 29.5 days, a bit longer than the 27-day orbit, because Earth moves around the Sun during that time and the Moon must catch up.
slides.title: Why the Moon Has Phases

bullets: **Waxing** means the lit part is growing; **waning** means it is shrinking
Sequence: new, crescent, first quarter, gibbous, full, then back down
A **lunar eclipse** happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow
A **solar eclipse** happens when the Moon blocks the Sun from part of Earth
slides.notes: Gibbous means more than half lit but not full. Eclipses are different from phases: a lunar eclipse really is Earth's shadow on the Moon. Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly relative to Earth's path around the Sun, so the three bodies rarely line up exactly.
slides.title: Waxing, Waning and Eclipses

bullets: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees from straight up relative to its orbit
Earth orbits the Sun once about every 365 days
The axis keeps pointing the same direction (toward Polaris) all year
Summer in a hemisphere: it tilts toward the Sun, giving longer days and higher Sun
slides.notes: Seasons come from tilt. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the Sun climbs higher and days are longer, so the ground gets more concentrated sunlight for more hours. Six months later, the Southern Hemisphere is the one tilted toward the Sun.
slides.title: Earth's Tilt Makes Seasons

bullets: Earth's orbit is nearly circular; the distance varies only by about 3 percent
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter
The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time
Solstices are the longest and shortest days; equinoxes have nearly equal day and night
slides.notes: If distance caused seasons, the whole planet would have summer at once. Instead, when it is summer in the United States it is winter in Australia. The summer solstice occurs around June 20 or 21 in the north, the winter solstice around December 21 or 22, and equinoxes around March 20 and September 22 or 23.
slides.title: Common Myth: Distance Does Not Cause Seasons

bullets: Earth's rotation (about 24 hours) causes day, night, and rising and setting
The Moon's orbit and our viewing angle cause phases over about 29.5 days
Earth's 23.5 degree tilt, plus its yearly orbit, causes seasons
Appearance is not always reality: motion in the sky is often our own motion
slides.notes: Everything we covered follows from three motions: Earth spinning, the Moon orbiting, and Earth orbiting with a tilt. When you look up, try to work out which motion is responsible for what you see. The next chapter turns to the planets that share our Sun.
slides.title: Summary: Three Ideas Explain the Sky

objectives: Explain why the Sun, Moon and stars appear to rise and set, using Earth's rotation.
Describe how the Moon's phases arise from the changing view of its sunlit half.
Predict the phase of the Moon from its position relative to the Sun and Earth.
Explain how Earth's axial tilt causes the seasons, and why distance from the Sun does not.
Apply these ideas to new situations, such as comparing day length in different places or seasons.
lesson.overview: This chapter starts with what you can see without any equipment: the Sun crossing the sky, the Moon changing shape, and the year turning from warm to cold and back. Each of these has a simple physical cause, and all of them come from the motions of just three bodies: Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. Understanding them gives you a mental model of how these bodies move, and you will use that model throughout the course. In Chapter 2 you will meet the other planets, which spin and orbit in similar ways, and in Chapter 3 you will see that the Sun is one star among countless others. For now, the goal is to look up and understand what is happening, using nothing more than patient observation and a few clear ideas.

steps: Start with what you know: Earth's circumference at the equator is about 40,000 km, and one rotation takes about 24 hours.
Use the speed formula: v = d / t, where v is speed, d is distance and t is time.
Put in the numbers: v = 40,000 km / 24 h.
Divide: 40,000 / 24 is about 1,670, so the speed is roughly 1,700 km/h.
Check that it makes sense: this is faster than a passenger jet, which is why it is surprising that we feel nothing.
example.takeaway: Earth's surface moves at roughly 1,700 km/h at the equator, but because everything around us moves with it, we feel no motion.
example.title: Worked example: How fast does the ground move at the equator?

keyTerms.def: The spinning of a body, such as Earth, around its own axis.
The imaginary line through a spinning body's poles around which it turns.
The North Star, a star that sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole and so appears nearly motionless in the northern sky.
The time for Earth to rotate once relative to the Sun, about 24 hours.
The line where the ground or sea appears to meet the sky.

misconception.fact: The Sun's daily path across the sky is caused by Earth rotating once about every 24 hours. The same rotation explains why the Moon and stars also rise and set, which would be a strange coincidence if each of them were circling Earth on its own.
misconception.myth: The Sun goes around the Earth every day, which is why it rises and sets.

choices: Earth rotates from west to east
Each object orbits Earth in a westward direction on its own schedule
Earth moves in a straight line toward the west
The sky is a dome that turns around us
practice.explanation: Earth's rotation toward the east makes the whole sky appear to move toward the west. The other choices describe separate motions for each object or motions that do not happen; one rotation explains everything at once.
practice.q: Why do the Sun, Moon and stars all appear to rise in the east and set in the west?

practice.answer: The Sun always lights half of Earth. Earth's rotation has carried my location into the half facing away from the Sun, so it is night for me. The Sun is still shining on the other side.
practice.explanation: A good answer says that the Sun lights only the half of Earth facing it, and that rotation turns your location away from it.
practice.q: Explain in two or three sentences why it is night where you are, without saying the Sun goes away.

choices: The place on the sky above Earth's North Pole, near Polaris
The Sun's position at midnight
The Moon
The east horizon
practice.explanation: The arcs are centered on the point in the sky directly above Earth's axis, which is near Polaris. The Sun, Moon and horizon positions all change and are not the center of the turning.
practice.q: A photographer points a camera at the northern sky and takes a long exposure. The stars appear as arcs around one point. What does that point most closely match in the Northern Hemisphere?

reading: Step outside on a clear day and watch the Sun for a few hours. It seems to climb the sky, cross it, and sink out of sight. For most of human history, people reasonably took this at face value: the Sun moves and the ground stays still. The ground certainly feels still. But the evidence points the other way. The Sun, Moon and stars appear to move across the sky because Earth is turning beneath them, and we are riding along on its surface.

Think of sitting on a slowly turning merry-go-round. The trees and buildings around the playground seem to drift past you, even though they are standing still. Your own motion makes the world look like it is moving the opposite way. Earth works the same way. We call Earth's turning **rotation**: it spins around an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, called its **axis**. One full rotation takes about 24 hours, which is the length of a day as we usually count it.

Day and night follow directly from this. The Sun lights up only the half of Earth facing it, just as a lamp lights one side of a ball in a dark room. As Earth rotates, your location carries you into the lit half, and you experience morning. Later you are carried out of it, and you experience evening and night. The Sun never switches off for night to happen; your part of the world simply turns away from it.

Which way does Earth spin? Seen from above the North Pole, it turns counterclockwise, which means it rotates from west to east. Because you are carried eastward, the sky appears to move westward. That is why the Sun, Moon and stars all rise in the east and set in the west. This is not a special rule for each object. It is one single effect of one single rotation.

The stars show the rotation especially well. In a long-exposure photograph pointed at the northern sky, the stars trace arcs, or circles, around one point. For a viewer in the Northern Hemisphere, that point is close to a star called Polaris, the North Star. Polaris sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole, so it stays nearly in place while everything else appears to turn around it. A viewer at the equator sees stars rise and set rather than circle, and the Southern Hemisphere has no bright star marking its pole.

How fast are you moving? Earth's circumference, the distance around it, is about 40,000 kilometers at the equator. Dividing by 24 hours gives roughly 1,700 kilometers per hour for someone standing on the equator. You do not feel this because you, the air and the ground all move together smoothly, the way you do not feel the motion of a plane cruising at a steady speed. Closer to the poles, the circle you travel is smaller, so you move more slowly.
sections.title: Day, night and the spinning Earth

steps: Recall the setup: at full moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon is on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun.
When the Sun sets in the west, the opposite part of the sky is just rising in the east.
So the full moon rises in the east at about the time the Sun sets in the west.
Through the night, the Moon crosses the sky, and it sets in the west around the time the Sun rises.
Conclusion: a full moon is visible all night long.
example.takeaway: A full moon sits opposite the Sun in the sky, so it rises at sunset and sets at sunrise.
example.title: Worked example: When does a full moon rise?

keyTerms.def: An object that orbits a larger object, such as the Moon orbiting Earth.
The shape of the Moon's lit part as seen from Earth at a given time.
The phase when the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun and its lit side faces away from us.
The phase when Earth is roughly between the Sun and the Moon and we see the Moon's entire lit face.
Waxing means the visible lit part is growing; waning means it is shrinking.

misconception.fact: Phases come from our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half as it orbits Earth. Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which happens only a few times a year at most, and only at full moon, while phases occur every month.
misconception.myth: The phases of the Moon are caused by Earth's shadow falling on it.

choices: Earth's shadow covers it
Its lit half faces away from Earth
It is too far from Earth
Clouds always block it then
practice.explanation: At new moon the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun, so the sunlit half faces away from us. Earth's shadow is not the cause, and distance does not change much during a month.
practice.q: At new moon, why can we not see the Moon?

practice.answer: Not for the side we see. At full moon, the half of the Moon lit by the Sun is the half facing Earth, so we see it fully lit. The far side is dark at that time, but we cannot see it from Earth.
practice.explanation: A good answer says that the Sun always lights one half of the Moon and that at full moon this lit half faces Earth.
practice.q: A friend says that half of the Moon is dark at full moon. Is that correct? Explain briefly.

choices: Around sunrise
Around midnight
Right at sunset
Around noon the next day
practice.explanation: A first-quarter moon is highest at sunset and sets around midnight. A moon that sets around sunrise would be a full moon, and one that sets near noon would be close to new.
practice.q: You step outside at sunset and see a first-quarter moon high in the southern sky. Roughly when will it set?

reading: The Moon is Earth's natural **satellite**, meaning an object that orbits a larger one. It is about 384,000 kilometers away on average and takes roughly 27 days to circle Earth once. Unlike the Sun, the Moon makes no light of its own. It shines because its surface reflects sunlight, much as a white wall glows when a flashlight hits it. At any moment, the Sun lights exactly half of the Moon, the half facing the Sun.

If half of the Moon is always lit, why does it change shape in the sky? The answer is about our viewpoint. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see its lit half from different angles. Sometimes we look at the lit side head-on, sometimes we see only a sliver of it, and sometimes we see none of it. These different views of the Moon's lit portion are called **phases**.

Picture holding a ball at arm's length in a dark room with a single lamp on one side. Turn slowly in a circle while keeping the ball in front of you. When the ball is on the far side of you from the lamp, you see its whole lit face. When it is between you and the lamp, you see its dark side. In between, you see part-lit shapes. You are Earth, the ball is the Moon, and the lamp is the Sun.

The main phases follow a regular order. At **new moon**, the Moon is roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it. A few days later a thin **crescent** appears. About a week after new moon is the first quarter, when we see half of the Moon's face lit. At **full moon**, about two weeks after new moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon, and we see the whole face lit. Then the phases run backward: third quarter, a thinning crescent, and new moon again.

The full cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days. This is longer than the 27-day orbit because Earth is also moving around the Sun during that time, so the Moon must travel a little extra to line up with the Sun again. The word *month* comes from the same root as *moon* and reflects this old connection between the calendar and the sky.

When the lit part is growing from night to night, we call the Moon **waxing**. When it is shrinking, we call it **waning**. Phases also affect when you can see the Moon. A full moon rises around sunset and sets around sunrise, so it is up all night. A first-quarter moon is highest in the sky around sunset and sets around midnight. A new moon travels across the sky with the Sun, so it is up in daytime and lost in the Sun's glare.
sections.title: The Moon and its phases

steps: Chicago is in the Northern Hemisphere and Sydney is in the Southern Hemisphere.
In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so Chicago has long days and a high Sun: summer.
At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so Sydney has short days and a low Sun: winter.
Six months later, in December, the situation reverses: Sydney has summer and Chicago has winter.
Conclusion: the two cities have opposite seasons at any given time.
example.takeaway: Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres show that tilt, not distance from the Sun, causes the seasons.
example.title: Worked example: Is it summer in Sydney when it is summer in Chicago?

keyTerms.def: The angle, about 23.5 degrees, between Earth's rotation axis and a line perpendicular to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
The path one object takes around another, such as Earth around the Sun.
One of the two days each year when a hemisphere is tilted most toward or away from the Sun, giving the longest or shortest day.
One of the two days each year when neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun and day and night are nearly equal in length.
A part of the year with a typical pattern of weather and daylight, caused by Earth's tilt.

misconception.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter, and the difference in distance is small. Seasons come from Earth's 23.5-degree tilt, which changes how high the Sun climbs and how long the days last. If distance were the cause, both hemispheres would have summer together.
misconception.myth: It is hot in summer because Earth is closer to the Sun then.

choices: The Moon has phases
Summer in Australia happens while it is winter in Canada
Days are longer at the equator
Polaris stays nearly fixed
practice.explanation: If distance caused seasons, the whole Earth would be in the same season at once. Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres point to tilt. The other observations are true but do not address the cause of seasons.
practice.q: Which observation best shows that distance from the Sun does not cause the seasons?

practice.answer: In winter the Sun is lower in the sky, so its light hits the ground at a slant. Like a flashlight beam at a slant, the same amount of light is spread over a larger area, so each patch of ground gets less heat. Days are also shorter, so there is less time to warm up.
practice.explanation: A good answer mentions a lower Sun, light spread over a larger area, and ideally shorter days.
practice.q: Explain why the Sun's light is less effective at heating the ground in winter, using the flashlight idea.

choices: Very strong seasons in each hemisphere
Opposite seasons in each hemisphere
Little or no seasonal change over the year
Seasons that depend on how fast it rotates
practice.explanation: Without tilt, neither hemisphere would lean toward or away from the star, so day length and Sun height would stay about the same all year. Strong or opposite seasons need a tilt.
practice.q: Imagine a planet with no axial tilt, orbiting its star in a nearly circular path. What would you expect about its seasons?

reading: Most people live somewhere with seasons: warm summers, cold winters, and milder spring and fall between. A common first guess is that summer happens when Earth is closer to the Sun. That guess is wrong. Earth's orbit is only slightly oval, and Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of Northern Hemisphere winter. The real cause is something else: Earth's tilt.

Earth's axis is not straight up and down relative to its path around the Sun. It is tilted by about 23.5 degrees. The key fact is that the axis keeps pointing toward the same place in space, near Polaris, throughout the year. Earth takes about 365 days to travel once around the Sun, an orbit. Because the tilt direction stays fixed while Earth moves, sometimes the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and six months later it leans away.

When the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, two things happen. First, the Sun climbs higher in the sky, so its light hits the ground more directly. Direct light is concentrated: think of shining a flashlight straight down on a table versus at a slant, where the slanted beam spreads over a larger, dimmer patch. Second, the days are longer, so the ground has more hours to absorb heat. Both effects together make summer warm.

In winter the reverse happens. The Northern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun, so the Sun stays lower in the sky, its light is spread thinner, and the days are shorter. Less heat arrives, and the weather is colder. The seasons in the Southern Hemisphere are opposite: when it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south, because one half leans toward the Sun while the other leans away. December in Australia is a summer month.

Four dates mark the year. The **solstices** are the days when the tilt is most extreme: around June 21 the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day, and around December 21 it has its shortest. The **equinoxes**, around March 20 and September 22, are the days when neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and day and night are close to equal length everywhere. The word equinox comes from Latin roots meaning equal night.

The tilt also explains some dramatic sights. Near the poles, summer brings days when the Sun does not set for weeks or months, and winter brings the reverse, a long stretch of darkness. At the equator, the Sun is always high and day length barely changes, so there are no strong seasons. This also gives you a test of the tilt idea. If distance caused seasons, the whole planet would have summer at once. Instead, the two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same moment, which only tilt can explain.
sections.title: Seasons

corrections.after: The Sun does not actually circle Earth each day; your location turns toward it and then away from it
corrections.before: The Sun does not move across the sky; your location turns toward it and then away from it
corrections.why: The Sun does appear to move across the sky. The point is that this daily motion is apparent, not real.

corrections.after: which happens only a few times a year at most, and only at full moon
corrections.before: which is rare and happens only at full moon
corrections.why: Lunar eclipses happen on average about twice a year, so calling them 'rare' overstates it. The intended contrast is that they are not monthly.
